--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: To determine the association of statin use with oncological outcomes and risk of pathologic upgrading following radical prostatectomy.
[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: Using a prospectively populated database of 3042 men who underwent open radical prostatectomy, patients were grouped according to reported statin use at the time of surgery. The primary outcome was time to biochemical recurrence. The secondary outcome was risk of pathologic upgrading among a subset of 1256 patients with Gleason pattern 3 + 3 = 6 on biopsy. A multivariable Cox model was used to assess risk of biochemical recurrence, and multivariable logistic regression was used to assess risk of pathologic upgrading.
[RESULTS]: Eight hundred twenty-four men (27%) reported statin use at the time of radical prostatectomy. Statin users were older and had higher body mass index, higher Charlson Comorbidity Index, and lower pretreatment prostate-specific antigen values than statin nonusers. Over a median follow-up of 70 months (interquartile range: 36-107), a total of 455 men (15%) experienced biochemical recurrence. Statin use was not associated with biochemical recurrence (adjusted hazard ratio: 1.06, 95% confidence interval: 0.86-1.31). Of those men with biopsy Gleason 3 + 3 = 6 disease, 647 (52%) were upgraded to higher grade disease following radical prostatectomy; however, statin use was not associated with pathologic upgrading (adjusted odds ratio: 0.78, 95% confidence interval: 0.58-1.04).
[CONCLUSION]: Preoperative statin use at the time of radical prostatectomy was not associated with biochemical recurrence or risk of pathologic upgrading in this cohort. These data add to the existing body of literature suggesting that statin use is not associated with more favorable clinical outcomes following radical prostatectomy.

key_findings.finding: The most directly relevant study is a 2016 prospective-database cohort of 3,042 men undergoing open radical prostatectomy: 824 (27%) reported statin use at surgery. Over median 70 months, 455 (15%) had biochemical recurrence; adjusted HR for preoperative statin use was 1.06 (95% CI 0.86–1.31), not statistically significant. In 1,256 men with biopsy Gleason 3+3=6, 647 (52%) were upgraded at prostatectomy; adjusted OR for upgrading with statin use was 0.78 (95% CI 0.58–1.04), also not statistically significant. This directly supports no demonstrable association with either outcome, although residual confounding and exposure misclassification are possible because use was reported at surgery and the cohort was observational.

source_tools.relevance: Direct human cohort evaluating both preoperative statin exposure, BCR, and biopsy-to-prostatectomy upgrading

key_findings.finding: Evidence for preoperative statins and biochemical recurrence is conflicting. In the SEARCH cohort (1,319 RP patients; 236 statin users at surgery; median follow-up 24–38 months), adjusted statin use was associated with lower PSA recurrence (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50–0.97; P=.03), with a dose pattern: HR 0.57 for simvastatin-equivalent 20 mg and HR 0.50 for >20 mg. Conversely, the NYU cohort (1,446 patients; 437 preoperative users; median follow-up 57 months) found no association (HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.82–1.61), and the pooled meta-analysis of that study plus five prior cohorts found HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.80–1.19).

source_tools.relevance: Adjusted positive preoperative association and dose-response from SEARCH
Null preoperative association and pooled meta-analysis

key_findings.finding: A separate 3,828-patient RP cohort found preoperative statin use lowered PSA modestly (median 5.0 vs 5.2 ng/mL; multivariable 4.7% decrease, P<.001) but was not associated with biochemical recurrence (P=.73; mean follow-up 26 months). This raises concern that statin-related PSA lowering could affect detection or apparent risk, but does not show worse oncologic outcomes.

source_tools.relevance: Large preoperative cohort reporting PSA effect and null BCR result

key_findings.finding: The Korean Asan cohort (2,137 RP patients) distinguished preoperative from postoperative exposure: preoperative users had lower PSA but no significant differences in organ-confined disease, pathologic Gleason score, or positive margins, and preoperative statin use did not significantly reduce BCR in stratified multivariable models. The apparent BCR benefit was associated with postoperative use through 36 months, especially in high-risk subgroups, so it should not be interpreted as evidence for preoperative exposure.

source_tools.relevance: Direct comparison of preoperative and postoperative statin exposure with pathologic outcomes and BCR

key_findings.finding: A 2020 single-center retrospective study of 875 RP patients (702 analyzed; 45.7% statin users at surgery) reported lower BCR with statins (HR 0.599, P<.05) over median 51.2 months, with stronger associations in pT2c and ISUP≥3 disease. However, the abstract does not establish a clearly preoperative-only exposure window, and the study is retrospective with likely treatment-selection/confounding concerns.

source_tools.relevance: Additional human RP cohort reporting a protective generic-statin association

key_findings.finding: Atorvastatin-specific randomized evidence is postoperative rather than preoperative: PRO-STAT randomized 364 high-risk RP patients to atorvastatin 20 mg/day or placebo for 1 year after surgery; 1-year BCR was 16.4% vs 16.0%, HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.58–1.60), not significant. Thus it does not answer whether preoperative atorvastatin use at RP affects BCR. A preoperative fluvastatin window study (33 men, 4–12 weeks before RP) measured apoptosis biomarkers, not BCR, and was not a comparative recurrence cohort.

source_tools.relevance: Atorvastatin randomized trial showing no postoperative BCR benefit
Preoperative statin intervention with biomarker rather than recurrence endpoint

key_findings.finding: The searched literature did not identify directly relevant human RP cohorts reporting separate outcome estimates for atorvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin, or rosuvastatin as individual preoperative agents. Most cohorts evaluate generic statin use; SEARCH additionally uses simvastatin-equivalent dose categories, not simvastatin-specific comparative effects. Therefore, drug-specific conclusions for those four agents are insufficient.

source_tools.relevance: Targeted searches for individual statins and statin types; results mainly generic-statin cohorts/reviews and no qualifying agent-specific preoperative RP outcome cohort
